title: Pronoms sujets et être
ruleNote: Every French sentence needs a subject pronoun (je, tu, il, elle, on, nous, vous, ils, elles) and a matching verb. This module pairs those pronouns with 'être' (to be), the most important irregular verb in French. Master these and you can already describe people, things, and yourself.

elements.label: Pronom sujet : je
elements.ruleNote: 'je' means 'I'. Before a vowel or silent h it shrinks to 'j'' (j'ai, j'aime), but with 'être' it stays 'je' (je suis).

examples.explanation: 'je' is the first-person subject, kept full before 'suis'.
'je' opens the sentence as the subject.

examples.prompt: Construis : « I am in the city. »
examples.explanation: 'je suis dans la ville' = 'I am in the city'.

elements.label: Pronom sujet : tu
elements.ruleNote: 'tu' means 'you' for one person you know well — a friend, a family member, a child. It is the informal singular 'you'.

examples.explanation: 'tu' is the informal 'you' for one person.
'tu es à la maison' = 'you are at home'.

elements.label: Pronoms sujets : il / elle
elements.ruleNote: 'il' means 'he/it' (masculine) and 'elle' means 'she/it' (feminine). They match the gender of the noun they replace.

examples.hint: A boy takes the masculine pronoun.
A girl takes the feminine pronoun.
A feminine noun is replaced by 'elle'.

elements.label: je suis / tu es
elements.ruleNote: The verb 'être' (to be) is irregular: 'je suis' (I am) and 'tu es' (you are). Learn these two forms together.

elements.label: il est / elle est
elements.ruleNote: For 'he is' and 'she is', both use the same form: 'il est' and 'elle est'. The verb does not change for gender.

examples.explanation: 'il est' goes with the masculine subject.

elements.label: Pronom sujet : on
elements.ruleNote: 'on' often means 'we' in everyday speech (on est ici = we are here). It always takes the same verb form as il/elle.

examples.hint: Which subject pairs with 'est' here for 'we'?

examples.prompt: Construis : « We are in the city. »
examples.explanation: 'on est dans la ville' = 'we are in the city'.

elements.label: Pronom sujet : nous
elements.ruleNote: 'nous' means 'we'. It is the formal or written 'we'; in casual speech French often prefers 'on'.

examples.prompt: Construis : « We are in the city. »
examples.explanation: 'nous sommes dans la ville' = 'we are in the city'.

elements.label: Pronom sujet : vous
elements.ruleNote: 'vous' means 'you' for several people, or one person formally (a stranger, a teacher). It is both plural and polite singular.

examples.prompt: Construis : « You are in the city. »
examples.explanation: 'vous êtes dans la ville' = 'you are in the city'.

elements.label: Pronoms sujets : ils / elles
elements.ruleNote: 'ils' is 'they' for a masculine or mixed group; 'elles' is 'they' for an all-feminine group. Even one man makes the group 'ils'.

examples.hint: All girls is the feminine group.

examples.prompt: Complète : « ___ sont ici. » (un homme et une femme)
examples.hint: One man makes the group masculine.

elements.label: nous sommes / vous êtes
elements.ruleNote: The plural forms of être: 'nous sommes' (we are) and 'vous êtes' (you are). Note the liaison: vous êtes sounds like 'vou-zêtes'.

examples.explanation: 'nous sommes à l'école' = 'we are at school'.

elements.label: ils sont / elles sont
elements.ruleNote: For 'they are', both ils and elles use 'sont': ils sont, elles sont. The verb form is the same for both genders.

examples.prompt: Construis : « They are in the city. »
examples.explanation: 'ils sont dans la ville' = 'they are in the city'.

elements.label: Conjugaison complète d'être
elements.ruleNote: All of être at once: je suis, tu es, il/elle est, nous sommes, vous êtes, ils/elles sont. Mixing persons trains the whole table.

elements.label: être + adjectif
elements.ruleNote: Use être to describe: je suis content, elle est grande. The adjective agrees with the subject's gender and number.

elements.label: être + nationalité / profession
elements.ruleNote: After être, give a nationality or a job with no article: il est français, elle est médecin. The word agrees in gender.

examples.explanation: A profession after 'est' takes no article.
examples.hint: No article before a job after il/elle est.

elements.label: C'est + nom
elements.ruleNote: Use 'c'est' (it is / this is) to point out one thing or person with an article: c'est un chien, c'est ma mère.

examples.explanation: Pointing at a thing with an article: 'c'est'.

elements.label: C'est vs Il/Elle est
elements.ruleNote: Use 'c'est' before a noun with an article (c'est un médecin) but 'il/elle est' before a bare adjective or profession (il est médecin).

elements.label: Ce sont (pluriel)
elements.ruleNote: The plural of c'est is 'ce sont': ce sont des amis. Use it to point out more than one thing or person.

elements.label: Tu es vs Vous êtes
elements.ruleNote: Same idea 'you are', two forms: 'tu es' to one friend, 'vous êtes' to several people or one person politely. Choose by relationship.

elements.label: être à la forme négative
elements.ruleNote: Make être negative by wrapping the verb in ne...pas: je ne suis pas, il n'est pas. The 'ne' becomes 'n'' before a vowel.

examples.prompt: Construis : « I am not at home. »

examples.explanation: 'pas' closes the negation after the verb.

elements.label: Synthèse : pronom + être
elements.ruleNote: Put it all together: pick the right subject pronoun, conjugate être correctly, and finish with an adjective, a noun (c'est), or a negation.

examples.explanation: 'je suis français' combines pronoun + être + nationality.

examples.prompt: Construis : « She is not at home. »

examples.explanation: Pointing with an article: 'c'est un chat'.
